summary: Two-author CMU narrative review and forward-looking essay on AI for requirements engineering (RE). It sketches the history of AI-for-RE, LLM advances (pre-training limits, reasoning, context management), prompt programming, generalist SE agents and spec-driven development (spec-first / spec-anchored / spec-as-source), then argues that as implementation gets cheaper RE shifts toward operational specs, context curation, verification and long-horizon evaluation.

claims.claim: As implementation becomes cheaper via SE agents, engineering effort shifts from writing code toward expressing, curating, verifying and evaluating requirements (a swing back toward plan-driven development).
claims.evidence: Argued in §1 and §5 from cited trade-press/analyst signals (e.g. a 2025 executive survey on headcount reductions, which the authors note is anticipatory) and secondary literature; no new data.

claims.claim: AI-for-RE research has mostly targeted requirements validation, with less work on verification (code/design satisfying requirements).
claims.evidence: Based on a review of SE/RE venues since 2020 that the authors state 'is not systematic nor is it comprehensive' (§2); no counts or coding scheme reported.

claims.claim: Context files and specs help or hurt agents depending on how they are written; unnecessary requirements reduce success and raise token use.
claims.evidence: Cites two prior studies ([113] reduced runtime/tokens; [66] irrelevant content reduces success) and CodeSpecBench best model 20.2% ([28]); secondary evidence accurately hedged as 'mixed'.

claims.claim: RE lacks long-horizon benchmarks covering elicitation, planning, trace preservation and requirements-satisfaction testing; BLEU/ROUGE, LLM judges and fluency-dominated human evaluation are inadequate.
claims.evidence: Research-agenda argument supported by cited metric critiques ([24,146,21,120,43,168]) and a cited NLG survey (200+ metrics, 478 evaluations, 165 papers [71]).

patterns.note: Describes SDD spectrum (spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source) and tools (SpecKit, Kiro, BMAD, OpenSpec); notes lack of evaluation frameworks and spec drift; no new evidence.
Mentions EARS-formatted requirements, Gherkin scenarios and acceptance tests as spec artifacts; calls for trace preservation to stakeholder acceptance tests.
Summarises secondary evidence that AGENTS.md-style context files can reduce runtime or reduce success depending on irrelevant content ([113] vs [66]).
Cites evidence that LLM judges give biased labels and near-random performance in some settings ([43],[168]); argues they do not solve RE evaluation.
Suggests recursive summarization, hierarchical memory or graph retrieval may be needed to keep agents adherent to growing requirements documentation.
Mentions executable behavioral specs, auto-formalization and offloading verification to provers/model checkers as future directions.

methodology.sample: Non-systematic narrative review of SE/RE venues since 2020 (TSE, TOSEM, REJ, ICSE, FSE, RE, ASE) plus LLM literature; ~200 references; no inclusion criteria or counts.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; no venue in comment or journal_ref.

biases.detail: Authors state the review 'is not systematic nor is it comprehensive' (§2); characterisations of the field cannot be checked.
Motivation rests on trade-press/analyst figures (executive survey 60%/21% headcount reductions; Copilot +26% task completion) that the authors themselves flag as anticipatory or possibly outdated.
Framing of an industry-wide 'transformation' and fewer developers orchestrating agents is forecast, not evidence.

coi.affiliations: Software and Societal Systems Department, Carnegie Mellon University (both authors).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None evaluated; SDD tools (SpecKit, Kiro, BMAD, OpenSpec) only mentioned.
coi.funding: No funding or acknowledgments section found.
coi.detail: Academic authors with no vendor ties evident.

verdict_reason: Useful, well-hedged framing of spec-driven development and RE evaluation gaps, but it is an explicitly non-systematic narrative essay with no new evidence; any empirical point should be traced to the cited primary studies, not this paper. Rigor 1 means the gate will reject it as evidence.
applicability: Framing only. For a Java team adopting spec-driven development across >=4 ingestion repositories, the spec-first vs spec-anchored vs spec-as-source distinction (§4.3) is a useful decision vocabulary: spec-anchored (specs versioned with code, alignment enforced by tests) is the variant that guards against drift between the ingestion repos and front-end delivery contracts. The paper's call for change-impact analysis and traceability over spec artifacts maps to cross-repo contract checks, and its warning that irrelevant content in context/spec files can hurt agents argues for keeping per-repo AGENTS.md/spec files minimal and host-neutral for mixed agent hosts. It offers no healthcare-specific or Java-specific evidence and no measured effect sizes.
